postedAt.postedAgoText: 2 weeks ago • Visible to anyone on or off LinkedIn

repost.content:
Emma Burleigh  at Fortune  reported on something worth sitting with. Goldman Sachs projects the U.S. power and grid sector will need about 500,000 more workers by 2030. Those jobs take three to four years of training, so the gap can't close quickly even if everyone tried.

Emma’s potential solution: "autonomous equipment and human-like robots might have to step in to help lighten the load if worker supply can't keep up."

The problem isn't too few jobs. It's too few people for the jobs that already exist. In manufacturing alone, more than a million roles are sitting unfilled right now.

You don't automate that work to push people out. You automate it because the people aren't there and the work still has to get done.

That's why we built Digit for materials handling first. Not the flashiest task on the floor, but one of the hardest to staff and one a warehouse can't run without.

The demand is real, it's measurable, and it's growing. The question isn't whether we need help on the floor. It's who can deliver it.

The bottleneck in humanoid robotics has never been demand. It's been supply.

We’ve had conversations within every sector of material handling. Automotives, pharmaceuticals, warehouses, third-party logistics providers. All of them are moving heavy, bulky material at scale, and none of them can find the workforce to do it. The demand was there before the robots were.

What's changed is the ability to meet it. RoboFab, Agility's manufacturing facility in Salem, Oregon, has the capacity to produce up to 10,000 robots per year. That's not a moonshot capacity number. It's what the near-term market actually requires.

The industry has spent years proving the technology works. The next question is whether it can be built at the scale the problem demands. We've built the answer to that question.

author.name: Peggy Johnson

postedAt.postedAgoText: 3 months ago • Visible to anyone on or off LinkedIn

repost.content:
Robots scoring near 90% in controlled settings succeed at just 12% of real-world tasks.

That's the gap Dr. Robert Ambrose, former Chief of NASA's Software, Robotics and Simulation Division, identifies in his new Fortune commentary — and it's the gap that separates a demo from a deployment.

His argument is one we've organized our company around: a humanoid is only as valuable as the hours it logs in a real production environment. Not a staged showcase. Actual shifts, in actual facilities, with customers depending on the work.

That's where Digit operates today.

Dr. Ambrose is also right that policy needs to catch up. Deployment-focused incentives and interoperability standards would unlock a market that's currently stuck in pilot purgatory.

The U.S. has the talent, the capital, and the industrial base to lead this transition. The question is whether we'll build for the demo or for the deployment.

We know which one we're choosing.

🤖 Digit-al Transformation: Toyota’s Humanoid Hire Changes the Equation

Toyota’s Canadian manufacturing subsidiary just contracted seven Agility Robotics Digit humanoids to work in their RAV4 production plant under a robots-as-a-service deal. After a year-long pilot, these robots will unload totes full of auto parts from automated warehouse tuggers - bridging the gap between two automated production lines.

🔑 Key Highlights:

🏭 Seven Digit humanoids deployed in live Toyota production environment after year-long pilot validation

🔄 Robots-as-a-service model reduces capital expenditure while proving commercial viability at scale

🎯 Agility leads real-world deployment with Digits working for GXO, Schaeffler, and Amazon beyond just pilots

💰 AI reducing deployment costs which “can be more than the price of the robot by a lot” per Agility’s CTO Pras Velagapudi  

Why This Deployment Matters:
	1.	Moving from lab demos to actual workflow integration proves humanoid economics work in real manufacturing environments
	2.	Robots-as-a-service model enables deployment without massive capital commitments, accelerating enterprise adoption
	3.	Next-generation robots designed for safe human collaboration unlock exponentially larger addressable market beyond isolated tasks

✍🏼 Demonstrating capability in a lab is one thing, but integrating humanoids into actual company workflows - including maintenance, charging, and daily operations - is where the real challenge lives. Toyota didn’t randomly pick Agility after their year-long pilot. They chose the company that’s already deployed with Amazon, GXO, and Schaeffler because real-world operational experience matters more than lab capabilities. The RaaS model proves critical here - companies can deploy without massive capital expenditure while Agility maintains the robots, handles software updates through their Arc platform, and continuously improves performance. 

What makes this even more significant is what comes next. Current humanoids are strong enough to lift heavy loads but still too unreliable to operate autonomously around people. The next-generation robots being designed for safe human collaboration will unlock the real opportunity - when they can work safely alongside humans across the entire factory floor, not just in isolated areas doing repetitive tasks. That’s when this goes from interesting pilot to structural transformation.

We’re back with a new episode of #FutureBackDrinking. This time I sat down with Peggy Johnson, CEO of Agility Robotics, for a conversation that went well beyond the mechanics of physical AI and into what this moment really means for how people and machines work together.
 
What stayed with me most is the clarity on where humans continue to lead. Even as robots become more capable — able to move, reason, and adapt in real-world environments — human judgment, creativity, and contextual decision-making remain unmatched. That advantage doesn’t disappear as technology advances; it becomes more important.
 
And as physical AI scales, the opportunity isn’t just about offloading repetitive or physically demanding work. It’s about what emerges next. Just as few could have predicted social influencing as a career path twenty years ago, we’re still only beginning to see the kinds of roles, skills, and ways of working that will take shape as humans and intelligent machines collaborate more closely.
 
That’s what makes this moment exciting. Not automation for its own sake, but augmentation that creates entirely new possibilities for work, growth, and impact.

repost.content:
Safety First. While speed is crucial in disruptive fields like humanoid robotics, it can never come at the cost of human safety. We must shift some of the industry focus from generating market hype to developing reliably safe, value added  products on behalf of customers.

Prioritizing safety means:

Ethical Commitment: Ensuring every employee and customer returns home safely, every single day.

Strategic Longevity: Recognizing that a robust safety culture is the most effective form of risk mitigation, safeguarding enterprise value.

Decisive Action: Empowering teams to issue an immediate, zero-debate Stop Work Order the moment a safety concern is raised.

If a leadership team must debate putting safety first, they lack the foundational integrity required for physical product development and ethics to lead large scale teams. 

Long-term success is built on trust, not on shortcuts and while Safety may not be sexy- it is exactly the first foundational element that Agility is building its technology upon.

repost.content:
Earlier this month, Digit hit the one-year mark working full-time for GXO Logistics, Inc.

During each shift, AMRs bring totes full of product to Digit's station from the order picking area. Digit unloads the AMR and loads the totes into a conveyor, where they zip off to pack-out stations.

When the downstream stations are backed up or employees are on a break, Digit will stack totes to the side instead of placing them in the conveyor. That way, the AMR flow continues through the facility. Once the conveyor is running again, Digit loads the queued-up totes and switches back to unloading the AMRs as they arrive.

It's a reliable and predictable form of labor. Even better, for the last nine months, there haven't been any Agility engineers needed on-site. An example of a truly deployed solution, no training wheels required.
